w: Reykjavik's concert hall opened on 4 May 2011 behind a facade of coloured glass, each hexagonal pane echoing the basalt columns that line Iceland's coast. Function follows form here -- acoustics tuned for orchestras, a skyline landmark for everyone else walking the harbour front after dark.
s: A concert hall wrapped in Iceland's own basalt geometry
_facts: Concert hall and conference centre in Reykjavik, opening concert held 4 May 2011
Distinctive coloured glass facade inspired by Iceland's basalt landscape

w: Built from hewn dolerite in 1880-81, this is where Althingi, the Icelandic parliament, still sits. Carved into four windows are the landvaettir -- dragon, vulture, giant, bull -- spirits calmed by Ingolfur Arnarson on landing, so the story goes. It also housed a library, gallery and, until 1973, the president's office.
s: Iceland's parliament, guarded by four carved spirits
_facts: Classical 19th-century building housing Althingi, the Icelandic parliament, built 1880-1881 from hewn Icelandic dolerite
Reliefs on four first-floor windows represent the four landvaettir of Iceland, said to have been momentarily appeased by Ingolfur Arnarson on his first landing
Has also housed the National Library, the National Gallery, the University of Iceland (1911-1940) and the president's offices (until 1973)

w: Six hot-water tanks on top of a hill, capped with a glass dome and opened to the public in 1991. Four tanks still heat the city; the other two became a planetarium with a Northern Lights show and a hundred-metre ice cave built from four hundred tons of ice, snow and ash. Ride the lift up for the 360-degree view.
s: A planetarium and ice cave built on hot-water tanks
_facts: Natural history museum on top of Öskjuhlíð hill, a glass dome resting on six district heating tanks, opened to the public 21 June 1991
Four tanks remain in use for heating; one became a 100-metre ice cave built from around 400 tons of ice, snow and ash, another a planetarium with a Northern Lights show
Also features a 360-degree observation deck and an interactive glacier exhibit

w: The mother church of Iceland's Lutheran faith sits right next to parliament on Austurvollur, and the two buildings have been in on the joke since 1845: every session of the Althingi opens with a Mass here, after which the dean walks the assembled MPs next door to actually get to work.
s: Where Iceland's parliament goes to Mass before voting
_facts: Seat of the Bishop of Iceland and mother church of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Iceland, located at Austurvollur next to the parliament house
Since the Althingi was resurrected in 1845, each parliamentary session has begun with a Mass at the cathedral

w: Founded in 1863 to finally give Iceland its own collection -- before then, the country's antiquities and treasures sat in Danish museums across the water. Jon Arnason took over as the first curator of the Icelandic collection, launching an institution that has run continuously for over a century and a half.
s: Iceland's treasures, finally kept in Iceland
_facts: Jon Arnason was the first curator of the Icelandic collection, which had previously been kept in Danish museums

w: Iceland's only Catholic cathedral, tucked into western Reykjavik and known locally as Landakotskirkja. Officially the Basilica of Christ the King, seat of the Diocese of Reykjavik -- and its congregation is the country's most international, with Mass said in Icelandic, Polish and English on rotation.
s: Iceland's only Catholic cathedral, three languages of Mass
_facts: Officially the Basilica of Christ the King, the sole Catholic cathedral in Iceland and seat of the Diocese of Reykjavik
Services are held in Icelandic, Polish and English
